name: City of London Cemetery
text: Your train passes near the City of London Cemetery, on the train's {side}, laid out in 1855 on land bought from the second Duke of Wellington, to take the burials of the City's 106 parishes. It covers 200 acres, is listed Grade I as a park and garden, and Bobby Moore's ashes are in its Garden of Remembrance.

name: Ilford Depot
text: Your train passes Ilford Depot, on the train's {side}, where trains for Greater Anglia, the Elizabeth Line and London Overground are kept and maintained. An engine shed opened here in 1901; the steel frame of the first shed of the present depot was up by June 1940, but it had no roof until 1949.

name: Seven Kings
text: Your train passes through Seven Kings, on the train's {side}, a district of Ilford by the old Roman road to Colchester that grew quickly once this railway was built. The name was first recorded as Sevekyngg in 1285, and may mean the settlement of the family or followers of a man called Seofoca.

name: Embassy Cinema
text: Your train passes near the Embassy Cinema, on the train's {side}, an art deco cinema at Chadwell Heath that opened on May 17th 1934 with 1,812 seats, most of it built in just 22 weeks. It closed in 1966 and became a bingo hall, and a project is now under way to restore it as a cinema.

name: Star Brewery
text: Your train passes near the site of the Star Brewery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1708 beside the Star Inn and later the home of Ind Coope. A tunnel under this railway linked it to the goods yard, and by 1970 it had 1,000 workers. It closed in 1993, and one of its chimneys stands in The Brewery shopping centre.

name: Romford Market
text: Your train passes near Romford Market, on the train's {side}, which began as a sheep market and was granted its market right by royal order in 1247. Cattle were last sold here in 1958; today it is an outdoor retail market, open on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays.

name: Langtons
text: Your train passes near Langtons, on the train's {side}, an 18th-century house in Hornchurch whose gardens, with a serpentine pond, a bath house and a gazebo, were laid out to the plans of Humphry Repton. The house is now the borough's register office, and the gardens a public park.

name: Hornchurch Cutting
text: Your train runs through Hornchurch Cutting, a geological Site of Special Scientific Interest found when this line was built in 1892. It marks the southern edge of the ice sheet of 450,000 years ago, which left five metres of boulder clay here, along with rocks and Jurassic fossils carried from the Midlands.

name: Upminster Windmill
text: Your train passes near Upminster Windmill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill built in 1803 for James Nokes of Hunt's Farm. It is listed Grade II*, and between 2016 and 2023 it was restored to working order, with a new visitor centre beside it.

name: Eastbury Manor House
text: Your train passes near Eastbury Manor House, on the train's {side}, built in the 1570s by the merchant Clement Sisley on land that had belonged to Barking Abbey. It was probably the first brick building in the area. A tradition, probably groundless, has the Gunpowder Plotters meeting here; the house belongs to the National Trust.

name: Barking Abbey
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Barking Abbey, on the train's {side}, a royal abbey of nuns founded in the seventh century and once one of the most important in the country. It lasted almost 900 years until it closed in 1539; its Curfew Tower, rebuilt in about 1460, still stands.

name: Rainham Hall
text: Your train passes near Rainham Hall, on the train's {side}, a Georgian house built in 1729 for Captain John Harle, with his and his wife Mary's initials worked into its wrought-iron railings. It belongs to the National Trust and appeared in the BBC's A Christmas Carol in 2019.

name: Church of St Helen and St Giles
text: Your train passes near the church of St Helen and St Giles in Rainham, on the train's {side}, built between 1160 and 1170 and the oldest building in the London Borough of Havering. Its Norman round-headed arches survive, and it is thought to look much as it did when it was built.

name: All Saints' Church, Cranham
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church in Cranham, on the train's {side}, where James Oglethorpe, the founder of the American state of Georgia, is buried with his wife in the chancel. The church was rebuilt on the old foundations, and his marble memorial is on the chancel's south wall.

name: Hare Hall
text: Your train passes near Hare Hall, on the train's {side}, a Palladian country house built in 1769 and 1770 to designs by James Paine. In the First World War its grounds were Hare Hall Camp, home to the second battalion of the Artists Rifles, and since 1921 it has housed the Royal Liberty School.

name: Forest Gate
text: Your train passes through Forest Gate, on the train's {side}, named after a gate across today's Woodford Road. It was put there to stop cattle straying from Wanstead Flats, part of Epping Forest, onto the old Roman road from London to Colchester.

name: Cann Hall
text: Your train passes near Cann Hall, on the train's {side}, an old manor that the daughter of Hugh de Montfort gave to the canons of Holy Trinity, Aldgate, in 1121. Its name is probably a shortening of Canons Hall, and the canons kept it until the Dissolution.

name: Leyton Cricket Ground
text: Your train passes near Leyton Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, the home of Essex County Cricket Club from 1886 to 1933. In June 1932 Herbert Sutcliffe and Percy Holmes of Yorkshire put on 555 here, then a world record partnership; its wooden pavilion is now listed.

name: St Barnabas Church, Walthamstow
text: Your train passes near St Barnabas Church in Walthamstow, on the train's {side}, built in 1902 and 1903 to a design by W. D. Caröe in the Arts and Crafts style, for the new Warner Estate. It is listed Grade II*, and has a chapel for St James's Church in St James Street, which closed in 1960.

name: Walthamstow Market
text: Your train passes near Walthamstow Market, on the train's {side}, which fills the High Street with about 500 stalls and dates from 1885. It is said to be the second longest outdoor market in Europe; it is often called a mile long, but is about a kilometre.

name: Walthamstow Wetlands
text: Your train passes Walthamstow Wetlands, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve on the reservoirs the East London Waterworks Company built here between 1853 and 1904. It is one of the largest urban wetland reserves in Europe, used by birds on migration, in winter and for breeding.

name: Harringay Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of Harringay Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened in 1927 as the third greyhound racing stadium in Britain, and used for speedway too. It was built on the site of a pottery works, and closed in 1987.

name: Walthamstow Pumphouse Museum
text: Your train passes near the Walthamstow Pumphouse Museum, on the train's {side}, in a sewage pumping station built in 1885. It tells of local firsts in transport, such as the first all-British aircraft, which flew from Walthamstow Marshes, and keeps a Victoria line carriage used for filming and concerts.

name: Walthamstow Power Station
text: Your train passes near the site of Walthamstow Power Station, on the train's {side}, which supplied the borough's electricity from September 20th 1901 until 1968. It stood in Exeter Street, with three brick chimneys and a row of wooden cooling towers.

name: Vestry House Museum
text: Your train passes near the Vestry House Museum, on the train's {side}, built in 1730 as the parish workhouse and later a police station. It is now Walthamstow's local history museum, and shows the Bremer Car, the first British motor car with an internal combustion engine, which first ran in 1892.

name: St Peter-in-the-Forest
text: Your train passes near St Peter-in-the-Forest, on the train's {side}, a church beside a small part of Epping Forest. It was built in 1840 in an Italianate style to a design by John Shaw Jr, and the right to choose its vicar has belonged to the Warner family since 1859.

name: Friday Hill House
text: Your train passes near Friday Hill House, on the train's {side}, a manor house built in 1839 by the architect Lewis Vulliamy and Robert Boothby Heathcote, who was lord of the manor and the local rector. The Heathcotes lived here until 1940, and a London plane in its grounds is one of the Great Trees of London.

name: Camden Market
text: Your train passes near Camden Market, on the train's {side}, which began as a temporary crafts market by Camden Lock in 1974, when a planned motorway ruled out any lasting building on the site. Partly in the old Pickfords stables, it now draws about 250,000 people a week.

name: Roundhouse
text: Your train passes the Roundhouse, on the train's {side}, built in 1846 and 1847 by the London and North Western Railway as an engine shed with a turntable, though used that way for only about a decade. It became an arts venue in 1964, and in 1968 it saw one of the Doors' only two British appearances with Jim Morrison.

name: Alexandra Road Estate
text: Your train passes the Alexandra Road Estate, beside the line, designed by Neave Brown in 1968 and built in white concrete between 1972 and 1978. Its eight-storey block next to the railway steps back like a ziggurat to shield the estate from the trains' noise, and its foundations rest on rubber pads against the vibration.

name: Kilburn Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Kilburn Priory, on the train's {side}, a small community of nuns founded in about 1130 where Watling Street, now Kilburn High Road, met the stream now called the Westbourne. The priory gave Kilburn its name, and Priory Road and Abbey Road are named after it.

name: Kensal Rise Library
text: Your train passes near Kensal Rise Library, on the train's {side}, opened in 1900 by Mark Twain, who was staying nearby at Dollis Hill House, on a site given by All Souls College, Oxford. When it was threatened with closure, Alan Bennett, Philip Pullman and Zadie Smith were among those who campaigned to save it.

name: Primrose Hill tunnels
text: Your train runs under Primrose Hill, through one of its tunnels. The first, driven through the London clay by Robert Stephenson for the London and Birmingham Railway and opened in 1838, was the first railway tunnel in London; a second followed in 1879, and a pair for the Watford DC line in 1912.

name: St Pancras Old Church
text: Your train passes near St Pancras Old Church, on the train's {side}, said to be one of the oldest places of Christian worship in England, though the evidence is thin. In its churchyard is the tomb John Soane designed for his wife and himself, which may have inspired the red telephone box, and Percy Shelley and the future Mary Shelley planned their elopement of 1814 at her mother's grave here.

name: Coal Drops Yard
text: Your train passes near Coal Drops Yard, on the train's {side}, two Victorian sheds that received coal from South Yorkshire and passed it on to narrowboats and horse-drawn carts, eight million tonnes a year. Redesigned by Thomas Heatherwick, they opened as shops in October 2018.

name: Isokon Flats
text: Your train passes the Isokon Flats, on the train's {side}, a block of modernist concrete flats designed by Wells Coates, opened on July 9th 1934 as an experiment in minimal living. Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer of the Bauhaus lived here, and so did Agatha Christie, from 1941 to 1947.

name: Westbere Copse
text: Your train passes Westbere Copse, on the train's {side}, a local nature reserve on railway land owned by Network Rail and leased to Camden Council. Mainly woodland of sycamore, oak, aspen and ash, it has recorded 25 species of birds and 150 of plants, and frogs, toads and newts too.

name: Oxgate Admiralty Citadel
text: Your train passes near the Oxgate Admiralty Citadel, on the train's {side}, a bunker built between 1937 and 1940 as a base for the Admiralty away from Whitehall. Above ground it is a three-storey building in the usual government style, with two basements below, the lower one specially protected; it was used from 1939 to 1944.

name: Welsh Harp railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Welsh Harp station, opened by the Midland Railway on May 2nd 1870 for Londoners coming out for fishing and boating on the Brent Reservoir. Named after a nearby inn, the Old Welsh Harp, it closed on July 1st 1903 and was soon demolished.

name: Royal Air Force Museum London
text: Your train passes near the Royal Air Force Museum, on the train's {side}, on the old Hendon Aerodrome, one of the first civilian airfields, acquired by Claude Grahame-White in 1911. Queen Elizabeth II opened the museum on November 15th 1972, with 36 aircraft in its hangars.
